newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' Ayala conglomerate sees steady rise.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' Ayala conglomerate sees steady rise.

text.p: The Philippines oldest conglomerate, Ayala Corp, expects net profits to grow by an average of 20 percent per year over the next five years, company president Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala said on Monday.

Ayala, 37, took over as president of the 162-year-old, family-controlled company from his father only last year. It is the most famous corporation in Philippine business, with holdings in the real estate, food, banking, insurance and telecommunications sectors.

"I would like to keep a pace of growing at 20 percent on the average on a yearly basis, say in the period of five years," Ayala told Reuters in an interview in his offices in the Ayala Tower, a landmark high-rise which also houses the Philippine Stock Exchange.
Ayala said analyst projections of 33 percent profit growth in 1996 "may be a little aggressive" but he added that he expected growth to be significantly higher than in 1995.

The conglomerate posted a net income of 4.18 billion pesos ($158.75 million) in 1995. A recent Reuters poll of five brokerage houses said its net income could grow by 33 percent to 5.56 billion pesos in 1996.
Both the 1995 figure and the forecast for 1996 exclude extraordinary gains.
"There's no doubt in my mind that very clearly we will grow significantly over last year ... Certainly, it will be comfortably over last year," Ayala said.

He also spoke of plans for the groups's various subsidiaries, including asset-rich Ayala Land Inc, which owns some 40 percent of the Makati commercial district, Bank of the Philippine Islands and Globe Telecom GMCR Inc, a joint venture with Singapore Telecom.
Ayala said he saw no downturn in Manila property values this year, despite analyst predictions of a slowdown after three years of steady price increases.
He said Ayala Land was attempting to unify leases on commercial properties in Makati so it could plan ahead for the time the leases run out.

He said he saw Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) matching Ayala Land's contributions to the group's bottom-line as it grew after a series of acquisitions. Ayala Land contributes some 60 percent ot the group's profits at present.
Ayala said BPI's income would grow faster after its latest merger with CityTrust Banking Corp last year since the merged bank would have a strong hold on the consumer banking business.
"Our consumer banking business is really going to take off with this merger," he said.
He said Globe Telecom would continue to lose money this year but the company was sure to post profits in 1998.
"I think we will still be in a loss situation this year. But I do believe that next year, 1998, there's absolutely no reason why we shouldn't be in the black," Ayala said.
Globe has earlier forecast a net loss of 321.2 million pesos this year from a net loss of 750.9 million last year.
The company was hit by a large number of fraudulent calls done by organised groups using sophisticated cloning devices.
"We were hit quite significantly by fraud last year. However, I do believe that those problems are behind us," Ayala added.
